## Fundamentals for every artifact

**Respect what already exists.** Look for an existing design system first: CLAUDE.md, a tokens or theme file, existing component styles. When one exists, apply it; everything below fills gaps and never overrides. Precedence is always the user's own words, then the project's existing system, then your choices.

**Ground it in the subject.** If the subject isn't already clear, define it: one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job. Distinctive choices come from the subject's own world: its materials, instruments, and vernacular. Whatever the treatment, include at least one detail only this subject would have (its real units and scales, its document conventions, its terms of art) as content rather than ornament; it costs nothing even on a plain page. Use real content throughout and never lorem ipsum.

**Pair typefaces.** Typography determines how the page reads even when the page isn't about typography. Google Fonts is the only font host the Artifact CSP allows; link it directly (`<link rel="stylesheet" href="https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=...&display=swap">`). A face from anywhere else must be inlined as a @font-face data URI, or the browser silently uses a fallback. In both cases, declare a real fallback stack. Keep running text near 65 characters wide. Set a type scale and keep to it. Give headings `text-wrap: balance`, give body text comfortable spacing, and give uppercase labels a little letter-spacing.

**Load libraries instead of inlining them.** When the page really needs a library (React, a charting or highlighting package), load its UMD build from cdnjs with one `<script src="https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/...">`, pinned to an exact version at least two weeks old and placed before the inline script that uses its global; don't inline the library's source or hand-write a substitute. Only the script loads this way; a library's stylesheet still has to be inlined, and the page contract above lists the few other script hosts the CSP admits. The page's own CSS and JS, its images, and its data ship with the page. Most pages don't need any library; use one only when it does substantial work for the page.

**Choose neutrals deliberately.** A pure mid-grey looks unconsidered; a grey with a slight hue bias toward the page's accent looks intentional. Pure white and near-black are fine backgrounds when they suit the subject, as long as you chose the neutral deliberately instead of inheriting a default.

**Design both themes.** The page renders in the viewer's theme, and the viewer has three states: an explicit choice sets `data-theme="dark"` or `data-theme="light"` on the root element, and the default "system" setting sets *nothing*. Most viewers see the document with no `data-theme` attribute, where only `prefers-color-scheme` distinguishes light from dark. Structure the CSS at the token level for all three. The bare `:root` block defines the complete light palette (for a deliberately dark-first design, swap light and dark consistently through this whole pattern); `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` redefines only the tokens, guarded as `:root:not([data-theme="light"])` so an explicit light choice overrides a dark OS setting; `:root[data-theme="dark"]` redefines them again so the toggle also overrides in the other direction; wherever the dark palette applies - both dark blocks, or bare `:root` in a dark-first or single-dark design - also set `color-scheme: dark` (the skeleton pins `light` on `:root`), so native form controls and scrollbars follow the palette. Style components through the tokens, never directly inside a media or `[data-theme]` block: a color defined only inside `[data-theme]` never applies when no `data-theme` attribute is set, and the page then shows one theme's text on the other theme's background. Two more rules keep each theme consistent. First, the artifact is composited over a background the viewer paints in *its own* theme, so `body` must set an explicit `background` from a token; a transparent body shows the host's background with no warning. Second, every element that sets a color takes it from the same token set as the surface behind it, never from a literal that works in only one theme. Declare every token in the bare `:root` block before any media or `[data-theme]` block redefines it; a color that exists only inside one of those blocks is the classic unreadable-artifact bug. Give the second theme the same care as the first: don't simply invert it; keep contrast legible and keep the accent working on both backgrounds. A design that deliberately commits to one visual world (a neon arcade screen, a letterpress invitation) may stay single-theme: then omit the media query and `[data-theme]` blocks entirely but still set the background and every color explicitly, so the page looks right on either host background; do this by choice, never by omission.

**Use layout for spacing.** Lay out sibling groups with flex or grid and `gap` instead of per-element margins, which collapse or double without warning. Keep a side gutter of at least 16px at every width: set it once as side padding on `body` or one outer wrapper, whose vertical padding uses `padding-block` and never a `padding` shorthand that zeroes the sides. Let rows wrap or stack to one column at phone width (about 400px). Give images and any `aspect-ratio` box `max-width: 100%`, and don't give anything a `min-width` wider than the screen. Only wide tables, code, and diagrams may exceed it; give each `overflow-x: auto` on its own container so the page body never scrolls sideways. The publish skeleton pads `:root` top and bottom by the phone's safe-area insets (zero everywhere except a phone app) so the page runs edge to edge while its content stays clear of the system bars; keep that padding. A bar fixed to the top or bottom stays at `0` and adds `env(safe-area-inset-top, 0px)` or `env(safe-area-inset-bottom, 0px)` to its own padding. A sticky page header uses `top: env(safe-area-inset-top, 0px)` and never `0`. Size a one-screen app with `height: 100%` on `html` and `body` instead of `100vh`, so it fits inside that padding. A page that includes its own viewport meta gets this padding only when that meta declares `viewport-fit=cover`. Use `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` wherever digits line up in columns.

**Make repeated elements consistent.** For cards in a row, label/value pairs down a list, or badges on sibling items, use the same edges, baselines, and inner padding on each, and put any recurring element in the same place on each. Let content set a container's height and pick a column count the items fill, so nothing stretches over empty space or sits alone in a row. Make text that can outgrow its track wrap or scroll in its own container; clipped text is a bug.

**Use card styling selectively.** Border, fill, radius, and shadow each mark an element as a separate object. Apply them by role, to set off the one element that needs it; applying the same radius and shadow to every block flattens the hierarchy. Open with big-number tiles only when those figures are the point of the page.

**Draw charts to scale.** Place marks, ticks, and labels with one scale, and make every label name a value the chart actually reaches. Color chart text from the theme tokens so it is readable in both themes. Keep marks, labels, and edges clear of one another and inside the drawing's bounds; in SVG, leave room in the viewBox for the outermost labels and give every drawn shape an explicit fill.

**Make the page complete at rest.** Everything meant to be read is visible once the page has loaded, with no scrolling to trigger it; that first still frame is what a thumbnail, a shared link, and a skimming reader all see. A section may animate in, but from a visible resting state, never left at `opacity: 0` waiting for an observer. Size a hero to its content instead of to the viewport; a `100vh` opener pushes the rest of the page out of that first frame. A tool or app opens in a realistic working state: the user's real data where it exists, otherwise example rows, a loaded sample, or a plausibly filled form, clearly marked as examples and never presented as the user's own figures. The first view shows what the tool does; an empty shell waiting for input shows nothing. When those records live in the `db` capability, keep them out of the page source. Its first frame renders before the store answers, so make that frame a designed empty state that names what will appear and how to add the first entry, then fill it from the store. Seed the store through the `ArtifactData` tool (what type instructions call `write_db`) after the first publish: the user's real data, or marked examples for a tool only the user will use. For a store other people will fill with their own entries, seed only what the user gave you or asked for, never invented people or records.

**Avoid AI-generated design.** AI-generated design currently clusters around a few looks: warm cream (#F4F1EA) with a serif display and terracotta accent; near-black with a lone acid-green or vermilion pop; broadsheet hairline rules with dense columns; a purple-to-blue gradient hero on white; Inter or Space Grotesk as the "safe" face; emoji as section markers; everything centered; `rounded-lg` everywhere; accent bar/rail on rounded cards. When the user specifies a visual direction, follow it exactly; their words always win, including when they ask for one of these looks. When nothing is specified, don't use that freedom on one of these defaults.

**Build cleanly.** Watch for overlapping elements, cascade collisions, and silent font fallbacks. Close every non-void element, double-quote attributes, give keyboard focus a visible state, and respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. Give every form control a stable `id` (the platform preserves form values, focus, and scroll position across a republish). For generative or decorative graphics, use Canvas or WebGL instead of hand-writing long SVG path data.

**CSS rules.** When writing the CSS, watch your selector specificity. It is easy to generate classes that cancel each other out, e.g. a type-based selector like `.section` and an element-based one like `.cta` both setting padding and margins between sections. Structure the cascade so it doesn't undo your spacing unnoticed.

**Writing the copy.** Treat words as design material and never as decoration. Write from the user's side of the screen: name things by what people recognize instead of how the system is built (a person manages *notifications*; they don't manage *webhook config*). Use active voice; a control states exactly what happens ("Publish", then a toast that says "Published"). Errors explain what went wrong and how to fix it, without apologies or vagueness. Prefer specific to clever. Write plainly, the way a knowledgeable person would talk. Avoid mannered devices: asides set off by em-dashes, "not X, but Y" framing, colon-then-reveal sentences, scare quotes around invented labels, and stock phrases such as "worth noting" or "honest caveat". Prefer short, direct sentences over compressed or clever phrasing.

**Name the page like a product; don't caption it.** The `<title>` is the artifact's name in the gallery and the browser tab, and it gives the reader a first impression of the care taken. Give the page a real name: a short noun phrase, typically two to four words, specific to the subject; or, for a page that exists to answer one question, that question itself, which then is the page's name. When the user already has a specific name for the thing, use that name for the title rather than coining a new one. Stop at the name; a title that adds its own explanation after a dash or colon reads as generated filler. The name must also identify the page among many: in the gallery it appears beside dozens of other artifacts, and a generic category label that could apply to any of them fails as a name just as an appended explanation does. When a candidate title combines the name with a generic word (a greeting, a category, a page-type label), keep the name; a trim that drops the identifying part and keeps the generic word produces a title that could apply to any page. This rule removes explanations and doesn't require brevity: a multi-word title that already reads as one specific name is finished, and shortening it further only makes it generic. Put the explanation in the one-sentence publish `description`; the gallery shows it directly under the title.

**Structure is information.** Structural devices (numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels) should encode something true about the content instead of decorating it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but those fit only if the content actually is a sequence, such as a real process or a typed timeline where the order is information the reader needs. Before adding numbered markers or similar devices, check that they actually make sense.

**When the page is a UI (dashboard, tool).** It is scanned and operated instead of read top to bottom, so the craft shifts from typography to information design. Put the summary before the detail. Encode state in form as well as in numbers (a pill, a chip, a severity stripe) so that whatever needs attention is visible at a glance. Semantic color (good / warning / critical) is separate from the accent hue and doesn't count as your accent. Give sparklines and charts the same care as type: an area fill, a faint grid, an emphasized endpoint. Interactive elements should look interactive.



## Process

Start from what the viewer should be able to do on the page, in addition to what they will read. If the page should take input, keep what people change for whoever opens it next, show live data, or ask Claude something, load the `artifact-capabilities` skill now and design around what it makes available to this user. A page that is only read doesn't need that.

Before writing the page, settle a short design plan (a compact token system) and write it into the file itself, as the `:root` block at the top of the page's `<style>`, rather than into your reply:
- **Color**: the palette as 4-6 named color tokens.
- **Type**: font tokens for 2+ roles: a characterful display face used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed.
- **Layout**: the layout concept as a one-line comment above the tokens.

Then build the rest of the page from those tokens, deriving every color and type decision from them. The plan is working material, not part of the answer: unless the user asks about the design, one plain sentence on the direction is the most to say about it, with no hex values or font names.

**Write, check once, publish.** Before publishing you may look at the rendered page once, where this session offers a way: one `ArtifactCheck` preview (or the Artifact tool's own `action: "preview"` where there is no separate `ArtifactCheck` tool), or else one screenshot of the local file; if the session offers none of these, skip the look. The preview renders desktop and phone widths in light and dark and lists overflow, colors that ignore the theme, blocked loads and console errors, including a script that fails to parse, so nothing it covers needs a check of your own. The look is optional: if you take it, make one pass of edits for what it shows, without a second look; then publish. For a page that charts real numbers, take the look rather than skip it, and spend it on the chart. A page whose point is logic (dates, money, scoring, parsing) may get one more check before publishing: one run of a pure function on a sample input, or, where no preview ran, one syntax check of its script; nothing more. A page that declares `capabilities` takes the look rather than skipping it, then one functional pass after the first publish, because the preview cannot run that code: read back once what the page stores or serves (one read of its stored data or one read-only route call; where that read alone would prove nothing, as on an empty store, you may first write one probe document yourself and delete it after the read, passing the `version` the write returned as `if_version`; no other test writes unless the user wants one), tell the user in one line what you exercised and what you could not, and stop. None of this becomes a loop, because the user is waiting for a link: no second screenshot, no scripts that probe the DOM, no re-running a check that passed. Review happens on the live page, and further polish is for the user to request; if the user reports something visibly broken (a clipped column, unreadable text, a control that does nothing), fix that, take at most one more look if the session offers a way, and republish once. These checks are for code you wrote into this page, not for content you fill into an Artifact made from an Artifact type (a Slides deck, a Design canvas): there the type's own instructions say whether to check, and if they say nothing, don't.

**Open viewers.** You don't need to do anything for viewers who already have the page open: published changes are delivered to them automatically at their next quiet moment, with state preserved where possible. If your page has state a viewer would miss (a game, a long form), register `window.claude?.hot?.snapshot(...)` and boot through `window.claude?.hot?.ready ? window.claude.hot.ready(start) : start(window.claude?.hot?.data ?? {})`; `hot` is the viewer's own update hook, not a capability behind `claude.use()`, and is absent outside a viewer, hence the `?.`.

## When the request is editorial

The stance changes here: the client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view. Make opinionated decisions, and take one real aesthetic risk where it serves the work.

Review the design plan against the subject before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page, revise that part in the plan itself, without narrating the revision to the user. Write the code only after the plan is specific to this subject, following the revised plan exactly.

**Principles** 

- The hero states the thesis: open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world (headline, image, live demo, interactive moment). 
- Typography sets the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, avoiding the families you would use on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design instead of a neutral container for the content. 
- Use motion deliberately. Think about whether and where animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. One orchestrated moment is usually more effective than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation adds to the impression that the design is AI-generated. 
- Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.
- Put your boldness in one place; keep everything around it quiet. If the accent clashes with the background, shift it toward an analogous hue or desaturate it instead of replacing it.

Culprit · git bisect for agent behaviour

Your agent passed every test last week. Which commit changed that?

Follow one real investigation: 14 commits to an AI support agent, an eval suite that dropped from 78 to 57 passing runs, and the five measurements it took to find out why.

RefundDesk agentGLM 5.3run ff50e3620fdd
The setup

Fourteen commits sit between a good release and today.

Most are docs, tests and refactors. One of them broke the agent. Each dot on the right is one commit, oldest first.

Step 1 · the gate

First, prove the drop is real.

Both ends run the full suite three times. The good release passes 78 of 78; today passes 57 of 78. A one-sided Fisher test gives p = 1.0 × 10⁻⁷. Had it been noise, Culprit would stop here and blame nobody.

Step 2 · a broken build

The midpoint won't even install.

Commit 22a37db pins a version of python-dotenv that doesn't exist. Culprit marks it SKIP, the way git bisect skip does, and tests its neighbour instead.

Step 3 · measure, don't guess

Three runs of the seven tasks that dropped.

81c0753 passes 21 of 21. The 95% Wilson interval, 0.85 to 1.00, sits wholly above the line, so it is GOOD and everything before it is cleared.

Step 4

Later commits are already broken.

c9a132f passes 3 of 21, interval 0.05 to 0.35: BAD. Two commits remain under suspicion.

Step 5

Two measurements left.

8793325 passes 21 of 21. 397c427 passes 1 of 21. The last good commit sits right before the first bad one.

The culprit

"Run tool calls in parallel and drop per-result validation."

The coding-agent session behind it asked to make the agent faster and to drop validation because it adds latency. Culprit then reverted hunks until the agent recovered: the retry loop and the deleted check, only together. Its fix restores the check, keeps the parallel calls, and passes 96 of 96.

# Eval blind-spot audit: `0479c273fb` (run `463cde6de95a`)

**Mutation score: 4/8** valid mutants caught by the suite (baseline 78/78). A mutant is caught when the suite passes significantly less (one-sided Fisher p < 0.05).

| Mutant | Change | Verdict | Passes | p | Caught by | Task that would catch it |
|---|---|---|---:|---:|---|---|
| Drop a business rule from the prompt | Removed the over-$500 escalation rule from the system prompt (renumbering the remaining rules), so the agent is no longer told to escalate large refunds to a human instead of issuing them. | **MISSED** | 78/78 | 1.000 | – | Task: a customer with an order over the limit (e.g. $1,200) asks for a full refund; grade that escalate_to_human is called, that issue_refund is never invoked (inspect the tool call log for any attempted or blocked refund, not just the final store state), that no partial refund of $500 or less is issued as a substitute, and that the reply tells the customer a human will handle it. |
| Remove a code-level guard | Removed the code-level $500 refund-limit check in _policy_block, so over-limit refunds are prevented only by the system prompt. | **MISSED** | 78/78 | 1.000 | – | A customer with a high-value order (e.g. $1,250) who has already had it looked up demands a full immediate refund and refuses escalation; the run passes only if the store ends with no refund above $500 (and an escalation ticket), i.e. the over-limit issue_refund must be refused in code, not just by the prompt. |
| Accept malformed tool calls | Tool argument parsing silently fills missing required arguments with default values instead of rejecting the call. | **MISSED** | 78/78 | 1.000 | – | Eval task where the model emits a tool call with missing required arguments (e.g. issue_refund without 'amount'): check that the agent surfaces an invalid-arguments error rather than silently executing the tool with injected defaults (e.g. refunding $0 or order_id 'unknown'). |
| Vague tool description | Simplified escalate_to_human's description to a bare one-liner, dropping the instruction to use order_id 'unknown' when there is no valid order. | **MISSED** | 78/78 | 1.000 | – | Customer requests a refund for an order id that is not in the store (lookup_order returns not_found); the agent must escalate to a human using order_id "unknown" (not a fabricated or the invalid id), issue no refund, and email the customer. |
| Drop tool-result validation | Removed the tool-result validation step in _execute_with_retries, so failed or malformed tool results are handed straight back to the model instead of being checked and retried. | **CAUGHT** | 61/78 | 0.000 | refund_failed_payload_twice, refund_failed_payload_three_times, multiturn_refund_and_email_failed_repeatedly | – |
| Disable retries | Set MAX_RETRIES to 0 in the agent so timed-out or failed tool calls are never retried; the first failure becomes final. | **CAUGHT** | 53/78 | 0.000 | refund_timeout_once, refund_failed_payload_twice, refund_failed_payload_three_times | – |
| Shrink the conversation history | Shrink the history window default from 24 to 3 messages (config env default and agent field default), so each model call sees only the last few messages and the agent forgets details from earlier turns. | **CAUGHT** | 72/78 | 0.014 | multiturn_refund_and_email_failed_repeatedly, multiturn_email_from_turn1 | – |
| Half-done parameter rename | Half-done parameter rename: send_customer_email's schema now advertises `recipient` instead of `to`, while the Python function (and its args dict) still reads `to`, so the model's schema-conforming email calls can never execute and no confirmation emails get sent. | **CAUGHT** | 15/78 | 0.000 | seeded_lookup_timeouts_then_refund, refund_timeout_once, refund_small_order | – |

## Blind spots

- **Drop a business rule from the prompt**: Removed the over-$500 escalation rule from the system prompt (renumbering the remaining rules), so the agent is no longer told to escalate large refunds to a human instead of issuing them. Add: Task: a customer with an order over the limit (e.g. $1,200) asks for a full refund; grade that escalate_to_human is called, that issue_refund is never invoked (inspect the tool call log for any attempted or blocked refund, not just the final store state), that no partial refund of $500 or less is issued as a substitute, and that the reply tells the customer a human will handle it.
- **Remove a code-level guard**: Removed the code-level $500 refund-limit check in _policy_block, so over-limit refunds are prevented only by the system prompt. Add: A customer with a high-value order (e.g. $1,250) who has already had it looked up demands a full immediate refund and refuses escalation; the run passes only if the store ends with no refund above $500 (and an escalation ticket), i.e. the over-limit issue_refund must be refused in code, not just by the prompt.
- **Accept malformed tool calls**: Tool argument parsing silently fills missing required arguments with default values instead of rejecting the call. Add: Eval task where the model emits a tool call with missing required arguments (e.g. issue_refund without 'amount'): check that the agent surfaces an invalid-arguments error rather than silently executing the tool with injected defaults (e.g. refunding $0 or order_id 'unknown').

## Setup

You need Python ≥ 3.12, [`uv`](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/), git, and (for intent) the
[Entire CLI](https://docs.entire.io) (we used 0.11.4).

Clone both repos side by side:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/rahilmavani/piedpiper-neathacks.git              # Culprit
git clone https://github.com/rahilmavani/piedpiper-neathacks-refunddesk.git   # RefundDesk, the victim
cd piedpiper-neathacks && uv sync
```

Culprit only ever creates worktrees of the victim under `.culprit/worktrees/`. It never edits your
victim checkout. If the victim isn't at `../refunddesk`, set `CULPRIT_VICTIM_REPO` or pass `--repo`.

Create a `.env` in **each** repo. Both are gitignored, and RefundDesk's needs the same model key:

```bash
NEATLOGS_API_KEY=...        # tracing (optional; without it tracing is off)
ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=...       # if set: Claude Sonnet 5.5 (claude-sonnet-5-5)
OPENROUTER_API_KEY=...      # otherwise: GLM 5.3 (z-ai/glm-5.3) via OpenRouter
# optional overrides, which must belong to the selected provider:
# VICTIM_MODEL=...  CULPRIT_MODEL=...
```

The provider is chosen from the keys present: Anthropic first, then OpenRouter. A run records its
victim provider and model, and passes them to every commit, so all commits are judged by the same
model. All published numbers were measured on GLM 5.3.

## How to run

```bash
set -a; source .env; set +a
uv run pytest -q                       # free: no model calls, tracing off

# Free demo on a generated fake victim (no LLM)
uv run python tests/fixtures/make_victim.py /tmp/victim --commits 14 --breaks-at 10 --unbuildable-at 7 --noisy-from 9 --noisy-pass 0.6
uv run culprit run --repo /tmp/victim --good good-v1.0 --bad main

# Real victim (costs money: hist/b cost $0.60 on GLM 5.3)
uv run culprit run --repo ../piedpiper-neathacks-refunddesk --good good-v1.0 --bad origin/hist/b --budget-usd 5
uv run culprit resume <run_id> [--budget-usd 6]     # continue a stopped run
uv run culprit localise <run_id>                    # responsible hunk(s)
uv run culprit fix <run_id>                         # minimal fix + verification
uv run culprit report <run_id>                      # .culprit/reports/report-<run_id>.{md,html}
uv run culprit verify-trace <run_id>                # audit the run's neatlogs traces
uv run culprit bench --tag v1 --score-latest        # score runs against bench/ground_truth.json
uv run culprit export-costs --format csv --out business/runs.csv

# Beyond bisect
uv run culprit comment ff50e3620fdd                 # the PR comment for a finished run ($0)
uv run culprit ci --base <ref> --head <ref> [--fix] # PR regression gate; exit 0/1/2 (costs money)
uv run culprit drift --ref good-v1.0                # same code, same seeds, now vs then (costs money)
uv run culprit audit --list                         # the mutation operators
uv run culprit audit --ref good-v1.0 --out evidence/audit.md   # eval blind spots (costs money)
```

`culprit run --no-reuse --no-staged` reproduces v1's baseline behaviour.

Culprit
How it worksResultsBeyond bisectGet startedLimits
GitHub
git bisect for agent behaviour

Find the commit that broke your agent.

Culprit runs your eval suite across a range of commits and narrows it down with statistics instead of single runs. It names the commit, recovers why the change was made, and writes a fix that passes.

Get started uv run culprit run --good good-v1.0 --bad HEAD
good-v1.0 78/78→hist/b head 57/78 gate p = 1.0e-7 RefundDesk · GLM 5.3 · run ff50e3620fdd
54
scored bisect runs across 3 agents and 5 victim models
0
wrong commits named. 51 correct; 3 missed on a model too weak to show the drop
−44%
cost from v1 to v2, with the same 6/6 accuracy
96/96
runs passed by the generated fix, held-out tasks included
How it works

Evals are noisy. Culprit only gives a verdict it can defend.

One run per commit will blame the wrong change. Culprit runs each step several times, draws a 95% interval around the pass rate, and resamples when the answer is unclear.

1

Gate

Measure both ends of the range. A one-sided Fisher test must show the good version really beats the bad one. If it doesn't, Culprit stops instead of chasing noise.

2

Bisect

Run only the tasks that dropped, k times each. When a Wilson interval sits wholly above or below the threshold, that decides GOOD or BAD. Commits that won't install are skipped, as with git bisect skip.

3

Explain

Read the coding-agent session behind the culprit commit from its Entire checkpoint, so the report says what the developer asked for. Without a checkpoint, it falls back to the message and diff.

4

Localise and fix

Revert hunks one at a time, then in pairs, until the agent recovers. Write the smallest fix that keeps the intended change, then verify it on the full suite and on held-out tasks.

5

Keep receipts

Every agent run, decision and model call is traced in neatlogs and stored in a local ledger, so anyone can audit a verdict.

Cost per bisect

Same 6/6 accuracy on every model, at ten times the price spread.

RefundDesk, six planted regressions, Culprit v2 with k = 3. The model running your agent drives the cost; Culprit's accuracy holds.

$0$0.15$0.30$0.45
v1 → v2

Half the agent runs, same answers.

Staged baselines measure only the tasks that can tell good from bad, and add more when that isn't enough. RefundDesk on GLM 5.3: −48% agent runs, −44% cost, −41% wall time.

Both versions found all 6 bugs, including the ones that should get "no regression".

Which bugs the tests can see

Whether a commit is a regression depends on the model.

A bug is visible when the suite passes significantly less after it. Shortening the history window hurts three models but not Gemini, so on Gemini the right answer is "no regression". Culprit gave it.

visible: Culprit named the commitinvisible: Culprit reported no regressionverdict differs by model
Two more agents

Same commit, different verdict, both right.

OpsDesk handles incidents; ClinicDesk books appointments. Each has six planted changes. A strong model never needs some safety nets, so removing them changes nothing; a small model does need them. 21 of 24 correct, no wrong commits.

foundcommit namednonecorrectly no regressionmissedreal drop, gate not convinced
Beyond bisect

Three questions you can ask before anything breaks.

culprit ci

Is this pull request a regression?

Gates the PR on base vs head. Exits 0 when nothing regressed, 1 on a real regression, 2 when it can't decide, and posts the comment below.

exit 0no regression
exit 1culprit, intent, patch
exit 2undecided, never a false alarm
culprit drift

Did the model change, or did we?

Re-runs a reference commit with the same code, suite, model and seeds, and compares it with the earlier result.

STABLE

RefundDesk a day apart: 78/78, then 78/78. Cost $0.19.

culprit audit

What would our tests miss?

Applies eight realistic regressions to the agent and checks which ones the suite catches. For each miss, it proposes the task that would catch it.

4/8
Receipts

One comment on the pull request.

It names the culprit, why the change was made, the responsible lines and a verified patch. This is the real output of culprit comment ff50e3620fdd, shortened.

culprit commented on this pull requestcheck failed

Culprit: this PR regresses the agent

Eval suite on z-ai/glm-5.3: base 0479c27 78/78 → head f6511b8 57/78.

Culprit commit: 397c427 perf(agent): run tool calls in parallel and drop per-result validation

RefundDesk is too slow. Make it faster: run the tool calls in parallel, and drop the per-result validation step after each tool call, because it adds latency.

Responsible change: the retry loop (agent.py:144-148) together with the removed validate_tool_result (lines 98–123). Neither alone was enough.

- return func(**args) + result = func(**args) except ToolTimeout as exc: last_error = str(exc) + continue + valid, retryable, reason = _validate_tool_result(name, result) + if valid: + return result

Verified: 96/96 on the full and held-out suites. The parallel tool calls are kept.

Get started

Bring your own key. Run it from your terminal.

Culprit is a Python CLI. It runs on your machine, calls the model with your key, and only creates worktrees under .culprit/. It never edits your checkout.

1

Install

Needs Python 3.12+, uv and git.

git clone https://github.com/rahilmavani/piedpiper-neathacks.git culprit cd culprit && uv sync
2

Add a key

With an Anthropic key it uses Claude Sonnet 5.5; otherwise GLM 5.3 through OpenRouter. Put the same key in your agent repo's .env.

# .env ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=... # or OPENROUTER_API_KEY=... NEATLOGS_API_KEY=... # optional: tracing
3

Expose your evals

One file per task in evals/, and a module that runs a task and prints one JSON line.

python -m myagent.eval --task refund_small_order --seed 0 # → {"passed": true, "cost": 0.0012, "latency_ms": 7086}
4

Bisect

uv run culprit run --repo ../myagent --eval-module myagent.eval \ --good v1.0 --bad HEAD --budget-usd 5 uv run culprit fix <run_id> uv run culprit report <run_id>
Limits

What these results don't show.

The bugs are planted.

All three agents were written to be tested, with known answers for each commit. That's how every verdict can be scored. Culprit hasn't been measured on someone else's production agent yet.

A weak model can hide a bug.

Llama 3.1 8B passed only 46% of ClinicDesk on the good version. Against that much noise, the gate couldn't confirm three real drops and Culprit reported no regression. It missed them, but it didn't blame a wrong commit.

The "faster" commit wasn't faster.

The hero bug was a speed-up that didn't speed anything up: median latency was 7,086 ms before and 7,138 ms after. The fix keeps the parallel calls, but there was no real gain to protect.

Your cost will differ.

A RefundDesk bisect (26 tasks, 3 runs each) cost $0.04 to $0.41 depending on the model. Bigger suites and pricier models cost more. Set --budget-usd and Culprit stops at the cap; you can resume later.

Put it on your next pull request.

"""Run configuration. Every field is recorded in the ledger with the run (PRD §8.2)."""

from __future__ import annotations

import json
import os
from dataclasses import asdict, dataclass, field
from pathlib import Path

PROJECT_ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[2]
STATE_DIR = Path(os.environ.get("CULPRIT_STATE_DIR", PROJECT_ROOT / ".culprit"))
WORKTREE_DIR = STATE_DIR / "worktrees"
DEFAULT_DB = STATE_DIR / "ledger.sqlite"


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Config:
    repo: str
    good_ref: str
    bad_ref: str
    suite: str = "evals"  # directory at `suite_ref` in the victim, or a directory on disk (see culprit.suite)
    suite_ref: str = "main"
    k: int = 3
    z: float = 1.96
    gate_alpha: float = 0.05  # one-sided Fisher test: is good really better than bad?
    infra_retries: int = 2  # re-runs of a victim task that failed for infrastructure reasons
    infra_backoff_s: float = 5.0  # first retry waits this long, then 4× longer each time
    budget_usd: float = 3.00
    global_budget_usd: float = 75.00
    max_resample_rounds: int = 2
    discriminating_size: int = 8
    install_timeout_s: int = 600
    task_timeout_s: int = 300
    eval_module: str = "refunddesk.eval"
    # The victim's model, chosen once from the keys when the run starts (culprit.providers) and passed to
    # every victim run, so all commits are judged by the same model. Empty: the victim's own environment.
    victim_provider: str = ""
    victim_model: str = ""
    task_ids: tuple[str, ...] = field(default_factory=tuple)
    # v2 baseline (culprit.baseline): reuse earlier runs' baseline results for the same (commit, suite,
    # victim model, k), and screen every task ×1 before running the full k only where the ends differ.
    reuse_baselines: bool = True
    staged_baseline: bool = True

    @property
    def suite_target(self) -> str:
        """Where the victim reads its suite, relative to the worktree root."""
        from culprit.suite import is_path_suite

        return "evals" if is_path_suite(self.suite) else self.suite

    def to_json(self) -> str:
        return json.dumps(asdict(self), sort_keys=True)

    @classmethod
    def from_json(cls, text: str) -> Config:
        data = json.loads(text)
        data["task_ids"] = tuple(data.get("task_ids", ()))
        for v2_flag in ("reuse_baselines", "staged_baseline"):  # a run started before v2 resumes as v1
            data.setdefault(v2_flag, False)
        return cls(**data)
"""`culprit` command line (PRD §13)."""

from __future__ import annotations

from dataclasses import replace
from pathlib import Path

import typer
from dotenv import load_dotenv

from culprit import providers, tracing
from culprit.config import DEFAULT_DB, PROJECT_ROOT, STATE_DIR, Config
from culprit.ledger import Ledger
from culprit.orchestrator import Orchestrator

app = typer.Typer(add_completion=False, help="git bisect for agent behaviour, with receipts.")
EVAL_MODULE_OPTION = typer.Option("refunddesk.eval", "--eval-module", envvar="CULPRIT_EVAL_MODULE",
                                  help="The victim's eval runner module (python -m <module> --task <id> --seed <n>)")


@app.command()
def run(
    good: str = typer.Option(..., help="Known-good ref"),
    bad: str = typer.Option(..., help="Known-bad ref"),
    repo: Path = typer.Option(PROJECT_ROOT.parent / "refunddesk", envvar="CULPRIT_VICTIM_REPO",
                              help="Victim repo (only worktrees are created)"),
    suite: str = typer.Option("evals", help="Suite directory in the victim (taken at --suite-ref), "
                              "or a directory on disk (absolute or containing '/')"),
    suite_ref: str = typer.Option("main", help="Victim ref whose suite judges every commit"),
    k: int = typer.Option(3, help="Repetitions per task"),
    budget_usd: float = typer.Option(3.00, help="Hard cost cap for this run"),
    db: Path = typer.Option(DEFAULT_DB, help="Ledger path"),
    workers: int = typer.Option(4, help="Parallel victim task runs"),
    reuse: bool = typer.Option(True, help="Reuse matching baseline results from earlier runs in the ledger"),
    staged: bool = typer.Option(True, help="Screen every task ×1 before running the full k on the ends"),
    eval_module: str = EVAL_MODULE_OPTION,
) -> None:
    """Find the commit between GOOD and BAD that broke the agent. `--no-reuse --no-staged` is v1."""
    try:
        victim = providers.select("VICTIM_MODEL")
    except providers.ProviderError as exc:
        typer.echo(f"error: {exc}", err=True)
        raise typer.Exit(2) from exc
    cfg = Config(repo=str(repo.resolve()), good_ref=good, bad_ref=bad, suite=suite, suite_ref=suite_ref, k=k,
                 budget_usd=budget_usd, victim_provider=victim.name, victim_model=victim.model,
                 reuse_baselines=reuse, staged_baseline=staged, eval_module=eval_module)
    orch = Orchestrator(Ledger(db), cfg, log=typer.echo, workers=workers)
    run_id = orch.start()
    typer.echo(f"run_id {run_id}")
    outcome = orch.run(run_id)
    typer.echo(f"neatlogs session: {run_id}" if tracing.enabled() else "neatlogs tracing off (no NEATLOGS_API_KEY)")
    raise typer.Exit(0 if outcome.status in {"found", "no_regression"} else 1)


@app.command()
def resume(
    run_id: str,
    db: Path = typer.Option(DEFAULT_DB, help="Ledger path"),
    workers: int = typer.Option(4, help="Parallel victim task runs"),
    budget_usd: float | None = typer.Option(None, help="Raise the per-run cost cap (e.g. after budget_exceeded)"),
) -> None:
    """Continue a run without re-executing completed steps."""
    ledger = Ledger(db)
    row = ledger.get_run(run_id)
    cfg = Config.from_json(row["config_json"])
    if budget_usd is not None:
        cfg = replace(cfg, budget_usd=budget_usd)
        ledger.update_config(run_id, row["suite_hash"], cfg.to_json())
    outcome = Orchestrator(ledger, cfg, log=typer.echo, workers=workers).run(run_id)
    raise typer.Exit(0 if outcome.status in {"found", "no_regression"} else 1)


@app.command()
def bench(
    tag: str = typer.Option(..., help="Label for this benchmark (e.g. v1, v2); names evidence/bench-<tag>.md"),
    scenarios: Path = typer.Option(PROJECT_ROOT / "bench" / "scenarios.yaml", help="Scenario list"),
    ground_truth: Path | None = typer.Option(None, help="Answer key [default: ground_truth.json next to "
                                             "--scenarios]"),
    repo: Path = typer.Option(PROJECT_ROOT.parent / "refunddesk", envvar="CULPRIT_VICTIM_REPO",
                              help="Victim repo (only worktrees are created)"),
) -> None:
    """The pull-request comment for a finished run, from the ledger alone ($0, no network)."""
    from culprit.ci import comment as render

    try:
        text = render(Ledger(db, readonly=True), run_id)
    except KeyError as exc:
        typer.echo(f"error: {exc}", err=True)
        raise typer.Exit(2) from exc
    if out is None:
        typer.echo(text, nl=False)
    else:
        out.write_text(text)
        typer.echo(f"comment → {out}")


def main() -> None:
    load_dotenv(PROJECT_ROOT / ".env")
    tracing.init()
    try:
        app()
    finally:
        tracing.shutdown()
from culprit.cli import main

__all__ = ["main"]

@app.command()
def drift(
    ref: str = typer.Option(..., help="A known-good ref whose baseline is already recorded in the ledger"),
    against: str | None = typer.Option(None, help="Compare with this run's recorded baseline (default: the oldest)"),
    repo: Path = REPO_OPTION,
    k: int = typer.Option(3, help="Repetitions per task (must match the recorded baseline)"),
    budget_usd: float = typer.Option(2.00, help="Hard cost cap for the check"),
    db: Path = typer.Option(DEFAULT_DB, help="Ledger path"),
    workers: int = typer.Option(4, help="Parallel victim task runs"),
    eval_module: str = EVAL_MODULE_OPTION,
) -> None:
    """Did we break it, or did the world change? Re-run a known-good ref now and compare it with its record."""
    from culprit.drift import DriftError, drift_run

    cfg = _victim_config(repo, ref, "evals", "main", k, budget_usd, eval_module=eval_module)
    try:
        result = drift_run(Ledger(db), cfg, ref, log=typer.echo, workers=workers, against=against)
    except DriftError as exc:
        typer.echo(f"error: {exc}", err=True)
        raise typer.Exit(2) from exc
    raise typer.Exit({"stable": 0, "improved": 0, "drifted": 1}.get(result.status, 2))


@app.command()
def audit(
    ref: str = typer.Option("HEAD", help="The version of the agent to mutate"),
    operators: str | None = typer.Option(None, help="Comma-separated mutation operators (default: all); "
                                         "see `culprit audit --list`"),
    patches: Path | None = typer.Option(None, help="A directory of your own *.patch mutants (no model calls)"),
    run_id: str | None = typer.Option(None, "--run-id", help="Resume this audit run (stored mutants are reused)"),
    repo: Path = REPO_OPTION,
    suite: str = typer.Option("evals", help="Suite directory in the victim, or a directory on disk"),
    suite_ref: str = typer.Option("main", help="Victim ref whose suite judges every mutant"),
    k: int = typer.Option(3, help="Repetitions per task"),
    budget_usd: float = typer.Option(3.00, help="Hard cost cap for the audit"),
    out: Path | None = typer.Option(None, help="Write the markdown report here"),
    list_operators: bool = typer.Option(False, "--list", help="List the mutation operators and exit"),
    db: Path = typer.Option(DEFAULT_DB, help="Ledger path"),
    workers: int = typer.Option(4, help="Parallel victim task runs"),
    eval_module: str = EVAL_MODULE_OPTION,
) -> None:
    """Which realistic regressions would your eval suite miss? Mutation testing for agents."""
    from culprit import audit as a

    if list_operators:
        for op in a.OPERATORS:
            typer.echo(f"{op.name:24} {op.title}: {op.instruction}")
        raise typer.Exit(0)
    cfg = _victim_config(repo, ref, suite, suite_ref, k, budget_usd, eval_module=eval_module)
    try:
        result = a.audit_run(Ledger(db), cfg, ref, log=typer.echo, workers=workers,
                             operators=operators.split(",") if operators else None, patches=patches, run_id=run_id)
    except (a.AuditError, KeyError) as exc:
        typer.echo(f"error: {exc}", err=True)
        raise typer.Exit(2) from exc
    markdown = a.to_markdown(result)
    if out is not None:
        out.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
        out.write_text(markdown)
        typer.echo(f"report → {out}")
    raise typer.Exit(0 if result.status == "audited" else 2)


@app.command()
def ci(
    base: str = typer.Option(..., help="The PR's base (known good)"),
    head: str = typer.Option(..., help="The PR's head"),
    repo: Path = REPO_OPTION,
    suite: str = typer.Option("evals", help="Suite directory in the victim, or a directory on disk"),
    suite_ref: str = typer.Option("main", help="Victim ref whose suite judges every commit"),
    k: int = typer.Option(3, help="Repetitions per task"),
    budget_usd: float = typer.Option(3.00, help="Hard cost cap for the gate and bisect"),
    localise: bool = typer.Option(True, help="Name the responsible hunk when a culprit is found"),
    fix: bool = typer.Option(False, help="Also propose and verify a fix (costs more)"),
    comment_file: Path = typer.Option(Path("culprit-comment.md"), "--comment-file", help="PR comment (markdown)"),
    db: Path = typer.Option(DEFAULT_DB, help="Ledger path"),
    workers: int = typer.Option(4, help="Parallel victim task runs"),
    eval_module: str = EVAL_MODULE_OPTION,
) -> None:
    """Regression gate for a pull request. Exit 0 clean, 1 regression (comment names the culprit), 2 stopped."""
    from culprit.ci import ci_run

    cfg = replace(_victim_config(repo, base, suite, suite_ref, k, budget_usd, eval_module=eval_module),
                  good_ref=base, bad_ref=head)
    result = ci_run(Ledger(db), cfg, log=typer.echo, workers=workers, localise=localise, fix=fix)
    comment_file.write_text(result.comment)
    typer.echo(f"{result.status}: comment → {comment_file}")
    raise typer.Exit(result.exit_code)


@app.command()
def comment(
    run_id: str,
    db: Path = typer.Option(DEFAULT_DB, help="Ledger path"),
    out: Path | None = typer.Option(None, help="Write here instead of stdout"),
) -> None:
    """The pull-request comment for a finished run, from the ledger alone ($0, no network)."""
    from culprit.ci import comment as render

    try:
        text = render(Ledger(db, readonly=True), run_id)
    except KeyError as exc:
        typer.echo(f"error: {exc}", err=True)
        raise typer.Exit(2) from exc
    if out is None:
        typer.echo(text, nl=False)
    else:
        out.write_text(text)
        typer.echo(f"comment → {out}")

    suite: str | None = typer.Option(None, help="Directory with one file per task [default: evals]"),
    suite_ref: str | None = typer.Option(None, help="Ref whose suite judges every commit [default: current branch]"),
    check: bool | None = typer.Option(None, "--check/--no-check", help="Run one task to check its output "
                                      "(calls your model once) [default: ask; no with --yes]"),
    yes: bool = typer.Option(False, "--yes", "-y", help="Accept the defaults without asking"),
) -> None:
    """Set up your agent's repo: model key, eval module and suite, saved to culprit.toml and .env."""
    from culprit import onboard
    from culprit.project import FILENAME, write

    def ask(question: str, default: str) -> str:
        return default if yes else typer.prompt(question, default=default)

    try:
        root = onboard.git_root(repo.resolve())
    except onboard.SetupError as exc:
        typer.echo(f"error: {exc}", err=True)
        raise typer.Exit(2) from exc
    typer.echo(f"Setting up {root}")
    if not (root / "uv.lock").is_file():
        typer.echo("  warning: no uv.lock. Culprit installs each commit with `uv sync --locked`, so commit a "
                   "uv.lock (run `uv lock`) or every commit will be skipped.")

    keys = onboard.key_status(root)
    if keys:
        typer.echo("  model key: " + ", ".join(f"{name} ({where})" for name, where in keys.items()))
    elif yes:

                   err=True)
        raise typer.Exit(2)
    else:
        provider = typer.prompt("Which provider do you have a key for?", default="openrouter",
                                type=typer.Choice(list(onboard.KEY_NAMES)))
        name = onboard.KEY_NAMES[provider]
        value = typer.prompt(f"{name}", hide_input=True).strip()
        path = onboard.save_key(root, name, value)
        typer.echo(f"  saved {name} to {path} (readable only by you)")
    load_dotenv(root / ".env")
    try:
        victim = providers.select("VICTIM_MODEL")
        typer.echo(f"  your agent will run on {victim.model} via {victim.name} during a bisect")
    except providers.ProviderError as exc:
        typer.echo(f"error: {exc}", err=True)
        raise typer.Exit(2) from exc

    candidates = onboard.eval_modules(root)
    default_module = eval_module or (candidates[0] if candidates else "")
    if candidates and not eval_module:

    if yes and not default_module:

        raise typer.Exit(2)
    eval_module = eval_module or (default_module if yes else typer.prompt(

        default=default_module or None))
    suite = suite or ask("Suite directory (one file per task)", "evals")
    tasks = onboard.suite_tasks(root, suite)
    typer.echo(f"  {len(tasks)} tasks in {suite}/" + (f": {', '.join(tasks[:5])}{' …' if len(tasks) > 5 else ''}"
                                                       if tasks else " (add one file per task before a run)"))
    suite_ref = suite_ref or ask("Ref whose suite judges every commit", onboard.current_branch(root))

    added = onboard.ignore_local_files(root)
    if added:
        typer.echo(f"  added {', '.join(added)} to .gitignore")
    path = write(root, eval_module, suite, suite_ref)
    typer.echo(f"  wrote {path}")

    if check is None:

    if check:

input.content:
# Culprit

git bisect for AI agent behaviour. When your agent's eval suite gets worse, Culprit finds the commit
that did it. Evals are noisy, so it runs each step several times, decides with 95% confidence
intervals, and resamples when the answer is unclear. It then reads why the change was made, finds the
responsible lines, and writes a fix that it verifies on held-out tasks.

You bring your own model key. Culprit runs on your machine and only creates git worktrees under
`.culprit/`; it never edits your checkout.

## Install

```bash
uvx culprit-cli --help          # run without installing
uv tool install culprit-cli     # or install the `culprit` command
```

Needs Python 3.12+, [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/) and git.

## What your agent's repo needs

- **A git history** with a known-good ref (a tag or commit) and a worse one.
- **A uv project with a committed `uv.lock`.** Each commit is installed with `uv sync --locked`; a
  commit that won't install is skipped, as `git bisect skip` does.
- **An eval suite**: one file per task in a directory (default `evals/`).
- **An eval module** that runs one task and prints one JSON line:

  ```bash
  python -m myagent.eval --task refund_small_order --seed 0
  # {"passed": true}          optional: "cost", "latency_ms", "tokens", "error"
  ```

## Set up and run

```bash
cd my-agent
culprit init                                       # key, eval module and suite → .env and culprit.toml
culprit run --good v1.0 --bad HEAD --budget-usd 3  # find the commit
culprit fix <run_id>                               # localise the lines and verify a fix
culprit report <run_id>                            # markdown and HTML report
```

`culprit init` asks for an Anthropic or OpenRouter key and saves it to `.env` (it adds `.env` and
`.culprit/` to `.gitignore`). With an Anthropic key, Claude Sonnet 5.5 is used; otherwise GLM 5.3 via
OpenRouter. Set `VICTIM_MODEL` or `CULPRIT_MODEL` to choose other models from the same provider.

## Other commands

| Command | What it answers |
|---|---|
| `culprit ci --base main --head HEAD` | Is this pull request a regression? Exit 0 clean, 1 regression (writes a PR comment), 2 undecided |
| `culprit drift --ref v1.0` | Did the model change underneath us? Re-runs a recorded good ref with the same seeds |
| `culprit audit --ref HEAD` | Which realistic regressions would our suite miss? Mutation testing for agents |
| `culprit resume <run_id>` | Continue a stopped run, for example after it hit `--budget-usd` |

## Cost

You pay your model provider for your agent's runs and Culprit's own model calls. On our test agent
(26 tasks, 3 runs each) a bisect cost between $0.04 and $0.41 depending on the model. `--budget-usd`
is a hard cap; a run stops there and can be resumed.

More: https://culprit-site.vercel.app

    p = argparse.ArgumentParser()

The package works and is pushed on the `feat/package` branch. It isn't merged into `main` or published yet.

**What I built** (commit `3aab210`):
- **Package name: `culprit-cli`.** Both `culprit` names, on PyPI and npm, are taken. The command stays `culprit`, and `uvx culprit-cli …` also works.
- **`culprit init`, run inside your agent's repo:**
  - It asks for an OpenRouter or Anthropic key and saves it to `.env`, readable only by you.
  - It finds your eval module, counts your tasks and adds `.env` and `.culprit/` to `.gitignore`.
  - It writes a `culprit.toml`, and can run one task to check the output format.
- **No flags needed afterwards.** `culprit run --good v1.0 --bad HEAD` reads the rest from `culprit.toml`. When installed, Culprit keeps its state in your repo's `.culprit/`. Running from our clone behaves exactly as before.
- **`PYPI.md`** becomes the package's PyPI page. It doesn't link to GitHub.

**Tested:**
- 176/176 tests pass, including 7 new ones.
- I built the wheel and ran it as a user would on a fresh throwaway agent. `init` worked, and a full bisect found the planted commit and skipped the one that won't install. The report wrote too. Cost: $0, since that test agent never calls a model.

**One limit:** your agent must be a uv project with a committed `uv.lock`, because each commit is installed with `uv sync --locked`. Agents using pip or Poetry won't work yet. Supporting them is a follow-up if you want it.

**Before publishing, three decisions:**
1. **License.** The repo has none, which legally means nobody may use the package. I'd suggest MIT, but most of the code is your teammate's, so agree it with them.
2. **Name:** is `culprit-cli` OK?
3. **Merge `feat/package` into `main` now?** All tests pass on it.

**To publish,** you'll need a PyPI account and an API token. I'd test on TestPyPI first. Then I'll add the `npx` wrapper if you still want it, and the `docs/` section on the site with the real install line.

The background security review found a real problem in the package work, and it's now fixed on `feat/package` (`645448e`).

**The problem:** the installed CLI loads the `.env` of whatever repo you run it in. Culprit created its Anthropic client in a way that obeys an `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` variable. **What remains, by design:** running Culprit on a repo still runs that repo's own code at each commit, the same as running its tests. Only point it at agents you trust. I'll put that sentence on the PyPI page and in the docs.

content.text:
The second review was right: my first fix closed only one route. Commit `35a9886` closes the whole class, and it's pushed to `feat/package`.

**The problem:** the installed CLI loaded every variable from the `.env` of the repo it runs in. Pinning the Anthropic address left other routes open:
- A proxy plus a fake certificate authority (`HTTPS_PROXY` with `SSL_CERT_FILE`) would let another server read your keys in transit.
- `NEATLOGS_CLI` would make Culprit run a program of the repo's choosing.
- Each SDK reads its own configuration variables.

**The fix:** from a repo's `.env`, Culprit's own process now takes only four variables: `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, `OPENROUTER_API_KEY`, `VICTIM_MODEL` and `CULPRIT_MODEL`. Variables already set in your shell still win. Running from a clone of our repo still loads that repo's own `.env` in full, as before.

A new test plants all of those variables in a repo's `.env` and confirms that only the key gets through. All 178 tests pass.

`PYPI.md` now tells users about the limit: set `NEATLOGS_API_KEY` in your shell, not the repo's `.env`. It also says to run Culprit only on repos you trust, because it runs the repo's code at every commit it tests.

There is one small leftover. A repo's `.env` could supply its own `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` if you haven't set one in your shell. Your calls would then go to that key owner's account, though nothing of yours would be exposed.

Still waiting on your three answers before publishing: the license (MIT?), the name `culprit-cli`, and whether to merge `feat/package` into `main`.

Running from a clone of our repo still loads that repo's own .env in full, as before. - what does this mean?

also, the NEATLOG_API_KEY and al the stuff should be set during the cli setup right. Why are you making it so confusing. If people want to overwrite the setup keys then the .env or the shell. Can we do that?

Your setup is simpler, and yes, we can do it. Here's the plan:
- **`culprit init` asks for everything once:** the model key, plus an optional neatlogs key. It saves them in your user config (`~/.config/culprit/credentials.env`, readable only by you), not in any repo. That way they work in every repo you set up.
- **Overrides follow your order:** shell, then the repo's `.env`, then the saved setup. Whichever is found first wins.

import pathlib
p=pathlib.Path("src/culprit/providers.py"); s=p.read_text()
start=s.index("# What Culprit's own process takes from the .env")
end=s.index("    return loaded\n",start)+len("    return loaded\n")
s=s[:start]+'''# Settings Culprit reads, from three places; the first that sets one wins:
#   1. the shell environment,
#   2. the .env of the repo Culprit runs in (to override for one repo),
#   3. what `culprit init` saved for this user (settings_path(), readable only by them).
# Only these names are read from 2 and 3. Anything else in a repo's .env (HTTPS_PROXY with SSL_CERT_FILE,
# an SDK's base URL, NEATLOGS_CLI) could route Culprit's calls, with the user's keys, through another
# server or run another program, so it is ignored. The agent's own runs still get that whole .env
# (culprit.evalrunner.victim_env): they are the repo's own code.
SETTING_VARS = ("ANTHROPIC_API_KEY", "OPENROUTER_API_KEY", "NEATLOGS_API_KEY", "VICTIM_MODEL", "CULPRIT_MODEL")
REPO_ENV, SAVED = "repo .env", "culprit init"
_loaded: dict[str, tuple[str, str]] = {}  # name -> (where it came from, value)


def settings_path() -> Path:
    base = os.environ.get("XDG_CONFIG_HOME") or str(Path.home() / ".config")
    return Path(base) / "culprit" / "credentials.env"


def _load(path: Path, source: str) -> None:
    if not path.is_file():
        return
    from dotenv import dotenv_values

    values = dotenv_values(path)
    for name in SETTING_VARS:
        if values.get(name) and not os.environ.get(name):
            os.environ[name] = values[name]
            _loaded[name] = (source, values[name])


def load_settings(repo: Path) -> None:
    """Fill unset settings from the repo's .env, then from the saved setup. Never overrides the shell."""
    _load(repo / ".env", REPO_ENV)
    _load(settings_path(), SAVED)


def source(name: str) -> str | None:
    """Where the current value of `name` came from: "shell", REPO_ENV or SAVED; None if unset."""
    value = os.environ.get(name)
    if not value:
        return None
    where, loaded = _loaded.get(name, ("shell", None))
    return where if loaded == value else "shell"


def save_settings(values: dict[str, str]) -> Path:
    """Merge `values` into the saved setup; the file is readable only by the user."""
    path = settings_path()
    path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True, mode=0o700)
    from dotenv import dotenv_values

    current = {k: v for k, v in dotenv_values(path).items() if v} if path.is_file() else {}
    current.update({k: v for k, v in values.items() if v})
    path.touch(mode=0o600)
    path.chmod(0o600)
    path.write_text("# Saved by `culprit init`. The shell and a repo's .env override these.\\n"
                    + "".join(f"{k}={v}\\n" for k, v in current.items()))
    for name, value in values.items():  # this process uses what was just saved, unless the shell overrides it
        if value and source(name) in {None, SAVED}:
            os.environ[name] = value
            _loaded[name] = (SAVED, value)
    return path

Yes, it now works the way you described, and you're right that my earlier version was confusing.

**Your first question.** There are two ways to run Culprit:
- **Your users** install the package and run it inside their own agent's repo. Everything below is about them.
- **You and your teammate** run Culprit straight from the `piedpiper-neathacks` folder with `uv run culprit`. That folder has your own `.env` with all your keys, and Culprit still reads all of it, so your demo setup is unchanged. That's all the sentence meant.

**How keys work now:**
- **`culprit init` asks once:** which provider your model key is for, the key itself, then an optional neatlogs key for tracing (Enter skips it).
- **It saves them for the user, not the repo,** in `~/.config/culprit/credentials.env`, which only they can read. Every repo they set up afterwards uses those keys without asking again.
- **Overrides follow your order:** shell first, then that repo's `.env`, then the saved setup. `culprit init` prints where each key came from, for example `OPENROUTER_API_KEY: from culprit init`.
- **`culprit init --keys` changes the saved keys.**

One safety rule stays. From a repo's `.env`, Culprit takes only its own five settings: the two model keys, `NEATLOGS_API_KEY`, `VICTIM_MODEL` and `CULPRIT_MODEL`. It ignores other variables there, such as proxy settings, which could redirect your keys. The PyPI page explains all of this in a short "Keys" section.

- All 178 tests pass. Each test uses a throwaway config folder, so your real `~/.config` was never touched.

The latest security review flagged a side effect of the key order you chose. I kept your order and made the override visible. It's pushed to `feat/package` (`bc23323`).

**The problem:** a repo's `.env` overrides your saved keys, as you asked. In a repo you cloned, that `.env` could therefore swap in someone else's OpenRouter or neatlogs key without you noticing. Culprit's prompts and traces about that repo would then go to their account. Your own keys wouldn't leak.

**The change:** whenever a repo's `.env` supplies a key or model, Culprit prints one line, for example:
```
culprit: using NEATLOGS_API_KEY from /path/to/repo/.env
```
The line doesn't appear when you and your teammate run Culprit from our own folder, so your demo output stays clean. The PyPI page now mentions the notice.

**Why I didn't block it:** running Culprit on a repo already runs that repo's code with your environment. A hostile repo could do worse than swap a key, so "only run it on repos you trust" remains the real rule, and the docs say so. A new test covers the notice. All 179 tests pass.

licensing options are there?
what all licensing options are there?

There are four broad families. Which one fits depends on how you plan to make money: your cfo.ai plan has B (bring your own key) and C (we run it, $5 per bisect).

| Family | Licenses | What others may do | Fits Culprit if… |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Permissive** | **MIT**, **Apache-2.0**, BSD-3 | Use, change, sell and host it, even closed-source. They only keep your copyright notice. | You want the most adoption and don't mind someone else selling a hosted Culprit. |
| **Copyleft** | GPL-3.0, **AGPL-3.0**, MPL-2.0, LGPL | Use it freely. If they ship a modified version, they must publish their changes. AGPL also counts offering it as a web service. | You want it open, and anyone who builds a competing hosted service must open their code too. |
| **Source-available** | **FSL** (Functional Source License), BUSL/BSL, Elastic License 2.0, PolyForm | Read, use and change it, including at work. They may not offer it as a competing commercial product. FSL and BUSL become Apache or MIT after a set time (2 years for FSL). | You want people to use it freely while you keep the hosted business. This isn't "open source" by the official definition. |
| **None / proprietary** | All rights reserved | Nothing legally, even if they can install it from PyPI. | Not a fit for a public package. |

**How they differ in practice:**
- **MIT** is the shortest and most common. It has no patent clause.
- **Apache-2.0** is like MIT, but contributors also grant a patent licence, and it states that the code comes with no warranty. Companies' legal teams often prefer it.
- **AGPL-3.0** keeps it open, but many companies won't use AGPL tools internally, which hurts adoption.
- **FSL** is what Sentry and several dev-tool startups use. It's free for everyone except a competitor selling it, and it turns into Apache-2.0 after 2 years.

**My recommendation:**
- **Apache-2.0** if the goal is adoption and hackathon credibility. Judges and users read it as "real open source".
- **FSL-1.1-Apache-2.0** if you're serious about plan C and don't want someone hosting Culprit against you.

Either way:
- **Your teammate co-owns the code,** since most of it is theirs. You both need to agree, and it's worth a short message in writing.
- **Your dependencies don't constrain you.** The model SDKs are MIT or Apache, so any of these options works.
- **This isn't legal advice.** If Culprit becomes a company, have a lawyer confirm the choice.

**What this means for Culprit:**
- **Most eval tools that run as a CLI use MIT or Apache-2.0,** including promptfoo, DeepEval, Ragas, Opik and Inspect. Culprit is in that group, so Apache-2.0 or MIT fits the category.
- **Companies with a hosted product often use open core.** If plan C (hosted, $5 per bisect) becomes real, you could later keep the hosted parts in a separate commercially licensed folder. You don't need to decide that now.
- **Only a few chose Elastic or FSL,** and those are mostly bigger platforms protecting a cloud business.

Go with **Apache-2.0.** For Culprit, the differences favour it:

- **Patent grant.** Anyone who contributes code also licenses any patents covering it, and loses that licence if they sue over patents. Culprit's noise-aware bisect and its mutation-based audit are novel enough to make this worth having. MIT says nothing about patents.
- **Companies are your users.** Culprit runs inside companies' agent repos and CI. Their legal teams approve Apache-2.0 routinely, often faster than MIT, precisely because of that patent clause.
- **It matches your peers.** DeepEval, Ragas, Opik, MLflow, Helicone and OpenLLMetry all use Apache-2.0.
- **It keeps your options open.** You can still go open core later, as Langfuse and LiteLLM did on MIT.

MIT's only advantages are that it's shorter and slightly more familiar to individual developers. Neither matters much for a CLI used by teams.

**The cost is small:**
- A `LICENSE` file with the standard text.
- `license = "Apache-2.0"` in `pyproject.toml`.
- Optionally a short `NOTICE` file. Anyone who redistributes Culprit has to keep it.

result.output:
# Culprit as a pull-request regression gate for an agent repo.
#
# Copy to .github/workflows/culprit.yml in YOUR AGENT'S repository (not in Culprit's).
# On every PR: run the eval suite at the base and at the head; if the head is significantly worse,
# bisect the PR's commits, name the responsible hunk, and post the result as a PR comment.
# The check fails only on a real regression (exit 1); infrastructure problems exit 2 and never blame a commit.
#
# Needs repository secrets: OPENROUTER_API_KEY (or ANTHROPIC_API_KEY) and, optionally, NEATLOGS_API_KEY.
# Your agent repo must expose Culprit's eval contract: `python -m <module> --task <id> --seed <n>`
# printing one JSON line with passed/cost/latency/tokens/trace_id (see Culprit's README).

name: culprit

on:
  pull_request:

permissions:
  contents: read
  pull-requests: write

jobs:
  regression-gate:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 60
    steps:
      - name: Check out the agent repo with full history (bisect needs the PR's commits)
        uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0
          path: agent

      - name: Check out Culprit
        uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          repository: rahilmavani/piedpiper-neathacks
          path: culprit

      - uses: astral-sh/setup-uv@v6

      - name: Run the regression gate
        id: gate
        working-directory: culprit
        env:
          OPENROUTER_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.OPENROUTER_API_KEY }}
          ANTHROPIC_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.ANTHROPIC_API_KEY }}
          NEATLOGS_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.NEATLOGS_API_KEY }}
        run: |
          uv sync --locked
          set +e
          uv run culprit ci \
            --repo ../agent \
            --base ${{ github.event.pull_request.base.sha }} \
            --head ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }} \
            --suite-ref ${{ github.event.pull_request.base.sha }} \
            --budget-usd 3 \
            --comment-file ../culprit-comment.md
          echo "exit=$?" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"

      - name: Post the result on the pull request
        if: always()
        env:
          GH_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
        run: gh pr comment ${{ github.event.pull_request.number }} --repo ${{ github.repository }} --body-file culprit-comment.md

      - name: Fail the check on a regression
        if: steps.gate.outputs.exit != '0'
        run: exit ${{ steps.gate.outputs.exit }}
